arXiv:0910.4991v2 [math.AP] 07 Nov 2009

On a maximum principle and its application to logarithmically critical Boussinesq system

Taoufik Hmidi Address: IRMAR, Université de Rennes 1
Campus de Beaulieu
35 042 Rennes cedex
France Email address: thmidi@univ-rennes1. fr
Abstract.

In this paper we study a transport-diffusion model with some logarithmic dissipations. We look for two kinds of estimates. The first one is a maximum principle whose proof is based on Askey theorem concerning characteristic functions and some tools from the theory of C0C_{0}-semigroups. The second one is a smoothing effect based on some results from harmonic analysis and sub-Markovian operators. As an application we prove the global well-posedness for the two-dimensional Euler-Boussinesq system where the dissipation occurs only on the temperature equation and has the form |D|logα⁡(e4+|D|)\frac{|\textnormal{D}|}{\log^{\alpha}(e^{4}+|\textnormal{D}|)}, with α∈[0,12]\alpha\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]. This result improves the critical dissipation (α=0)(\alpha=0) needed for global well-posedness which was discussed in [15].

1. Introduction

The first goal of this paper is to study some mathematical problems related to the following transport-diffusion model with logarithmic dissipations

(1) {∂tθ+v⋅∇θ+κ​|D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|)​θ=0,(t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝddiv​v=0θ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta+\kappa\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}\theta=0,(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ \theta_{|t=0}=\theta_{0}.\end{array}\right.

Here, the unknown is the scalar function θ\theta, the velocity vv is a time-dependent vector field with zero divergence and θ0\theta_{0} is the initial datum. The parameter κ≥0\kappa\geq 0, λ>1\lambda>1 and α,β∈ℝ.\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}. The operator |D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|)\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)} is defined through its Fourier transform

ℱ⁡(|D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|)​f)​(ξ)=|ξ|βlogα⁡(λ+|ξ|)​(ℱ​f)​(ξ).\mathcal{F}({\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}f})(\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\xi|)}(\mathcal{F}f)(\xi).

We will discuss along this paper some quantitative properties for this model, especially two kinds of information will be established: maximum principle and some smoothing effects. We notice that the special case of the equation (1) corresponding to α=0\alpha=0 and β∈[0,2]\beta\in[0,2] appears naturally in some fluid models like quasi-geostrophic equations or Boussinesq systems. In this context A. Córdoba and D. Córdoba [8] established the a priori LpL^{p} estimates: for p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty] and t≥0t\geq 0

(2) ‖θ⁡(t)‖Lp≤‖θ0‖Lp.\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}.

We remark that the proof in the case p=+∞p=+\infty can be obtained from the following representation of the fractional Laplacian |D|β|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta},

|D|β​f​(x)=cd​∫ℝdf⁡(x)−f⁡(y)|x−y|d+β​𝑑y.|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}f(x)=c_{d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}dy.

Indeed, one can check that if a continuous function reaches its maximum at some point x0x_{0} then |D|β​f​(x0)≥0|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}f(x_{0})\geq 0 and hence we conclude as for the heat equation. Our first main result si a generalization of the result of [8] to (1)

Theorem 1.1.

Let κ≥0,d∈{2,3},β∈]0,1],α≥0,λ≥e3+2​αβ\kappa\geq 0,d\in\{2,3\},\beta\in]0,1],\alpha\geq 0,\lambda\geq e^{\frac{3+2\alpha}{\beta}} and p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty]. Then any smooth solution of (1) satisfies

‖θ⁡(t)‖Lp≤‖θ0‖Lp.\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}.
Remark 1.2.

The restriction on the parameter β\beta is technical and we believe that the above theorem remains true for β∈]1,2[\beta\in]1,2[ and α>0.\alpha>0.

Let us discuss the proof in the special case of v≡0.v\equiv 0. The equation (1) is reduced to the fractional heat equation

∂tθ+κℒθ=0withℒ:=|D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|)⋅\partial_{t}\theta+\kappa\,\mathcal{L}\,\theta=0\quad\hbox{with}\quad\mathcal{L}:=\small{\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}}\cdot

The solution is explicitly given by the convolution formula

θ⁡(t,x)=Kt⋆θ0​(x)withKt^​(ξ)=e−t​|ξ|βlogα⁡(λ+|ξ|).\theta(t,x)=K_{t}\star\theta_{0}(x)\quad\hbox{with}\quad\widehat{K_{t}}(\xi)=e^{-t\frac{|\xi|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\xi|)}}.

We will show that the family (Kt)t≥0(K_{t})_{t\geq 0} is a convolution semigroup of probabilities which means that ℒ\mathcal{L} is the generator of a Lévy semigroup. Consequently, this family is a C0C_{0}-semigroup of contractions on LpL^{p} for every p∈[1,∞[.p\in[1,\infty[. The important step in the proof is to get the positivity of the kernel KtK_{t}. For this purpose we use Askey’s criterion for characteristic functions, see Theorem 3.4. We point out that the restrictions on the dimension dd and the values of β\beta are due to the use of this criterion. Now to deal with the full transport-diffusion equation (1) we use some results from the theory of C0−C_{0}-semigroups of contractions.

The second estimate that we intend to establish is a generalized Bernstein inequality. Before stating the result we recall that for q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} the operator Δq\Delta_{q} is the frequency localization around a ring of size 2q2^{q}, see next section for more details. Now our result reads as follows,

Theorem 1.3.

Let d∈{1,2,3},β∈]0,1],α≥0,λ≥e3+2​αβd\in\{1,2,3\},\beta\in]0,1],\alpha\geq 0,\lambda\geq e^{\frac{3+2\alpha}{\beta}} and p∈]1,∞[.p\in]1,\infty[. Then we have for q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} and f∈𝒮⁡(ℝd),f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

2q​β​(q+1)−α​‖Δq​f‖Lpp≤C​∫ℝd(|D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|)​Δq​f)​|Δq​f|p−2​Δq​f​𝑑x.{2^{q\beta}(q+1)^{-\alpha}\|\Delta_{q}f\|_{L^{p}}^{p}\leq C{\displaystyle{\int}}_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Big(\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}\Delta_{q}f\Big)\,|\Delta_{q}f|^{p-2}\Delta_{q}fdx.}

where CC is a constant depending on p,α,βp,\alpha,\beta and λ\lambda.

The proof relies on some tools from the theory of Lévy operators or more generally sub-Markovians operators combined with some results from harmonic analysis.

Remarks 1.4.
  1. (1)

    When α=0\alpha=0 then the above inequality is valid for all β∈[0,2].\beta\in[0,2]. The case β=2\beta=2 was discussed in [9, 25]. The remaining case β∈[0,2[\beta\in[0,2[ was treated by Miao et al. in [7] but only for p≥2.p\geq 2.

  2. (2)

    The proof for the case p=2p=2 is an easy consequence of Plancherel identity and does not require any assumption on the parameters α,β\alpha,\beta and λ\lambda.

The second part of this paper is concerned with an application of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 to the following Boussinesq model with general dissipation

(3) {∂tv+v⋅∇v+∇π=θ​e2,(t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ2∂tθ+v⋅∇θ+κ​ℒ​θ=0div​v=0v|t=0=v0,θ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v+\nabla\pi=\theta e_{2},\,\,(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta+\kappa\,\mathcal{L}\,\theta=0\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ v_{|t=0}=v_{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta_{0}.\end{array}\right.

Here, the velocity field vv is given by v=(v1,v2)v=(v^{1},v^{2}), the pressure π\pi and the temperature θ\theta are scalar functions. The force term θ​e2\theta e_{2} in the velocity equation, with e2e_{2} the vector (0,1)(0,1), models the effect of the gravity on the fluid motion. The operator ℒ\mathcal{L} whose form may vary is used to take into account anomalous diffusion in the fluid motion. From mathematical point of view, the question of global well-posedness for the inviscid model, corresponding to κ=0,\kappa=0, is extremely hard to deal with. We point out that the classical theory of symmetric hyperbolic quasi-linear systems can be applied for this system and thus we can get the local well-posedness for smooth initial data. The significant quantity that one need to bound in order to get the global existence is the L∞L^{\infty}-norm of the vorticity defined by ω=curl ​v=∂1v2−∂2v1.\omega=\mbox{curl }v=\partial_{1}v^{2}-\partial_{2}v^{1}. Now we observe from the first equation of (3) that ω\omega solves the equation

(4) ∂tω+v⋅∇ω=∂1θ.\partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega=\partial_{1}\theta.

The main difficulty encountered for the global existence is due to the lack of strong dissipation in the temperature equation: we don’t see how to estimate in a suitable way the quantity ∫0T‖∂1θ‖L∞\int_{0}^{T}\|\partial_{1}\theta\|_{L^{\infty}}. However, the situation in the viscous case, κ>0\kappa>0 and ℒ=−Δ\mathcal{L}=-\Delta, is well-understood and the question of global existence is solved recently in a series of papers. In [5], Chae proved the global existence and uniqueness for initial data (v0,θ0)∈Hs×Hs,(v_{0},\theta_{0})\in H^{s}\times H^{s}, with s>2,s>2, see also [18]. This result was improved by the author and Keraani in [13] to initial data v0∈Bp,12p+1v_{0}\in B_{p,1}^{\frac{2}{p}+1} and θ0∈Bp,1−1+2p∩Lr,r>2\theta_{0}\in B_{p,1}^{-1+\frac{2}{p}}\cap L^{r},r>2. The global existence of Yudovich solutions for this system was treated in [10]. We also mention that in [11], Danchin and Paicu constructed global strong solutions for a dissipative term of the form ∂11θ\partial_{11}\theta instead of Δ​θ.\Delta\theta. In the papers [17, 15] we try to understand the lower dissipation ℒ=|D|α\mathcal{L}=|\textnormal{D}|^{\alpha} needed for global existence. In [17] the author and Zerguine proved the global well-posedness when α∈]1,2[.\alpha\in]1,2[. The proof relies on the fact that the dissipation is sufficiently strong to counterbalance the possible amplification of the vorticity due to ∂1θ.\partial_{1}\theta. However the case α=1\alpha=1 is not reached by the method and this value of α\alpha is called critical in the sense that the dissipation and the amplification of the vorticity due to ∂1θ\partial_{1}\theta have the same order.

In [15] we prove that there is some hidden structure leading to global existence in the critical case. More precisely, we introduced the mixed quantity Γ=ω+∂1|D|​θ\Gamma=\omega+\frac{\partial_{1}}{|\textnormal{D}|}\theta which satisfies the equation

∂tΓ+v⋅∇Γ=−[ℛ,v⋅∇]θ.withℛ:=∂1|D|.\partial_{t}\Gamma+v\cdot\nabla\Gamma=-[\mathcal{R},v\cdot\nabla]\theta.\quad\hbox{with}\quad\mathcal{R}:={\frac{\partial_{1}}{|\textnormal{D}|}}.

As a matter of fact, the problem in the framework of Lebesgue spaces is reduced to the estimate the commutator between the advection v⋅∇v\cdot\nabla and Riesz transform ℛ\mathcal{R} which is homogenous of degree zero. Since Riesz transform is a Calderón-Zygmund operator then using in a suitable way the smoothing effects for θ\theta we can get a global estimate of ‖ω⁡(t)‖Lp\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}}. One can then use this information to control more strong norms of the vorticity like ‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} or ‖ω⁡(t)‖B∞,10\|\omega(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}. For more discussions about the global well-posedness problem concerning other classes of Boussinesq systems we refer to [16, 24].

Our goal here is to relax the critical dissipation needed for global well-posedness by some logarithmic factor. More precisely we will study the logarithmically critical Boussinesq model

(5) {∂tv+v⋅∇v+∇π=θ​e2∂tθ+v⋅∇θ+|D|logα⁡(λ+|D|)​θ=0div​v=0v|t=0=v0,θ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v+\nabla\pi=\theta e_{2}\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta+\frac{|\textnormal{D}|}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}\theta=0\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ v_{|t=0}=v^{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta^{0}.\end{array}\right.

Before stating our result we will need some new definitions. First, we define the logarithmic Riesz transform ℛα\mathcal{R}_{\alpha} by ℛα=∂1|D|​logα⁡(λ+|D|).\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}=\frac{\partial_{1}}{|\textnormal{D}|}{\tiny}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}. Second, for a given α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} we define the function spaces {𝒳p}1≤p≤∞\{\mathcal{X}_{p}\}_{1\leq p\leq\infty} by

u∈𝒳p⇔‖u‖𝒳p:=‖u‖B∞,10∩Lp+‖ℛα​u‖B∞,10∩Lp<∞.u\in\mathcal{X}_{p}\Leftrightarrow\|u\|_{\mathcal{X}_{p}}:=\|u\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{p}}+\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}u\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{p}}<\infty.

Our result reads as follows (see section 2 for the definitions and the basic properties of Besov spaces).

Theorem 1.5.

Let α∈[0,12],λ≥e4\alpha\in[0,\frac{1}{2}],\lambda\geq e^{4} and p∈]2,∞[p\in]2,\infty[. Let v0∈B∞,11∩W˙1,pv_{0}\in{B}_{\infty,1}^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p} be a divergence free vector-field of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and θ0∈𝒳p\theta_{0}\in\mathcal{X}_{p}. Then there exists a unique global solution (v,θ)(v,\theta) to the system (5) with

v∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,B∞,11∩W˙1,p),θ∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,𝒳p)∩L~loc1​(ℝ+,Bp,∞1,−α).v\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}\big(\mathbb{R}_{+};{B}_{\infty,1}^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p}),\qquad\theta\in L_{\textnormal{loc}}^{\infty}\big(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathcal{X}_{p}\big)\cap\widetilde{L}_{\textnormal{loc}}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};{B}_{p,\infty}^{1,-\alpha}).

The proof shares the same ideas as the case α=0\alpha=0 treated in [15] but with more technical difficulties. We define ℛα=∂1|D|​logα⁡(λ+|D|)\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}=\frac{\partial_{1}}{|\textnormal{D}|}{\tiny}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)} and Γ=ω+ℛα​θ.\Gamma=\omega+\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta. Then we get

∂tΓ+v⋅∇Γ=−[ℛα,v⋅∇]θ.\partial_{t}\Gamma+v\cdot\nabla\Gamma=-[\mathcal{R}_{\alpha},v\cdot\nabla]\theta.

To estimate the commutator in the framework of Lebesgue spaces we use the para-differential calculus combined with Theorems 1.1 and 1.3.

Remarks 1.6.
  1. (1)

    We point out that for global well-posedness to the generalized Navier-Stokes system in dimension three, Tao proved in a recent paper [28] that we can improve the dissipation |D|52|\textnormal{D}|^{\frac{5}{2}} to |D|52log12⁡(2+|D|)⋅\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\frac{5}{2}}}{\log^{\frac{1}{2}}(2+|\textnormal{D}|)}\cdot

  2. (2)

    The space 𝒳p\mathcal{X}_{p} is less regular than the space B∞,1ε∩Bp,1ε,∀ε>0.B_{\infty,1}^{\varepsilon}\cap B_{p,1}^{\varepsilon},\forall\varepsilon>0. More precisely, we will see in Proposition 4.3 that B∞,1ε∩Bp,1ε↪𝒳p.B_{\infty,1}^{\varepsilon}\cap B_{p,1}^{\varepsilon}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{X}_{p}.

  3. (3)

    If we take θ=0\theta=0 then the system (5) is reduced to the two-dimensional Euler system. It is well known that this system is globally well-posed in HsH^{s} for s>2s>2. The main tool for global existence is the BKM criterion [2] ensuring that the development of finite-time singularities for Kato’s solutions is related to the blowup of the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the vorticity near the maximal time existence. In [31] Vishik extended the global existence of strong solutions to initial data belonging to Besov spaces Bp,11+2/p.B_{p,1}^{1+2/p}. Notice that these spaces have the same scale as Lipschitz functions and in this sense they are called critical and it is not at all clear whether BKM criterion can be used in this context.

  4. (4)

    Since Br,11+2/r↪B∞,11∩W˙1,pB_{r,1}^{1+2/r}\hookrightarrow{B}_{\infty,1}^{1}\cap\dot{W}^{1,p} for all r∈[1,+∞[r\in[1,+\infty[ and p>max⁡{r,2}p>\max\{r,2\}, then the space of initial velocity in our theorem contains all the critical spaces Bp,11+2/pB_{p,1}^{1+2/p} except the biggest one, that is B∞,11B_{\infty,1}^{1}. For the limiting case we have been able to prove the global existence only up to the extra assumption ∇v0∈Lp\nabla v_{0}\in L^{p} for some p∈]2,∞[p\in]2,\infty[. The reason behind this extra assumption is the fact that to obtain a global L∞L^{\infty} bound for the vorticity we need before to establish an LpL^{p} estimate for some p∈]2,∞[p\in]2,\infty[ and it is not clear how to get rid of this condition.

  5. (5)

    Since ∇v∈Lloc1​(ℝ+,L∞)\nabla v\in L^{1}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\infty}) then we can propagate all the higher regularities: critical (for example v0∈Bp,11+2/pv_{0}\in B_{p,1}^{1+2/p} with p<∞p<\infty) and sub-critical (for example v0∈Hsv_{0}\in H^{s}, with s>2s>2).

2. Notations and preliminaries

2.1. Notations

Throughout this paper we will use the following notations.

∙\bullet For any positive AA and BB the notation A≲BA\lesssim B means that there exist a positive harmless constant CC such that A≤C​BA\leq CB.

∙\bullet Pour every p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], ∥⋅∥Lp\|\cdot\|_{L^{p}} denotes the norm in the Lebesgue space LpL^{p}.

∙\bullet The norm in the mixed space time Lebesgue space Lp​([0,T],Lr​(ℝd)CLOSEL^{p}([0,T],L^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is denoted by ∥⋅∥LTp​Lr\|\cdot\|_{L^{p}_{T}L^{r}} (with the obvious generalization to ∥⋅∥LTp​𝒳\|\cdot\|_{L^{p}_{T}\mathcal{X}} for any normed space 𝒳\mathcal{X}).

∙\bullet For any pair of operators PP and QQ on some Banach space 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the commutator [P,Q][P,Q] is given by P​Q−Q​PPQ-QP.

∙\bullet For p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], we denote by W˙1,p\dot{W}^{1,p} the space of distributions uu such that ∇u∈Lp.\nabla u\in L^{p}.

2.2. Functional spaces

Let us introduce the so-called Littlewood-Paley decomposition and the corresponding cut-off operators. There exists two radial positive functions χ∈𝒟⁡(ℝd)\chi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and φ∈𝒟⁡(ℝd\{0})\varphi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\backslash{\{0\}}) such that

  • i)

    χ⁡(ξ)+∑q≥0φ⁡(2−q​ξ)=1\displaystyle{\chi(\xi)+\sum_{q\geq 0}\varphi(2^{-q}\xi)=1};∀q≥1,supp ​χ∩supp ​φ​(2−q)=∅\quad\displaystyle{\forall\,\,q\geq 1,\,\textnormal{supp }\chi\cap\textnormal{supp }\varphi(2^{-q})=\varnothing}

  • ii)

    supp φ(2−j⋅)∩supp φ(2−k⋅)=∅,\textnormal{supp }\varphi(2^{-j}\cdot)\cap\textnormal{supp }\varphi(2^{-k}\cdot)=\varnothing, if |j−k|≥2|j-k|\geq 2.

For every v∈𝒮′​(ℝd)v\in{\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) we set

Δ−1​v=χ⁡(D)​v;∀q∈ℕ,Δq​v=φ⁡(2−q​D)​v and ​Sq=∑j=−1q−1Δj.\Delta_{-1}v=\chi(\hbox{D})v~;\,\forall q\in\mathbb{N},\;\Delta_{q}v=\varphi(2^{-q}\hbox{D})v\quad\hbox{ and }\;S_{q}=\sum_{j=-1}^{q-1}\Delta_{j}.

The homogeneous operators are defined by

Δ˙q​v=φ⁡(2−q​D)​v,S˙q​v=∑j≤q−1Δ˙j​v,∀q∈ℤ.\dot{\Delta}_{q}v=\varphi(2^{-q}\hbox{D})v,\quad\dot{S}_{q}v=\sum_{j\leq q-1}\dot{\Delta}_{j}v,\quad\forall q\in\mathbb{Z}.

From [4] we split the product u​vuv into three parts:

u​v=Tu​v+Tv​u+R⁡(u,v),uv=T_{u}v+T_{v}u+R(u,v),

with

Tuv=∑qSq−1uΔqv,R(u,v)=∑qΔquΔ~qvandΔ~q=∑i=−11Δq+i.T_{u}v=\sum_{q}S_{q-1}u\Delta_{q}v,\quad R(u,v)=\sum_{q}\Delta_{q}u\tilde{\Delta}_{q}v\quad\hbox{and}\quad\tilde{\Delta}_{q}=\sum_{i=-1}^{1}\Delta_{q+i}.

For (p,r)∈[1,+∞]2(p,r)\in[1,+\infty]^{2} and s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} we define the inhomogeneous Besov space Bp,rsB_{p,r}^{s} as the set of tempered distributions uu such that

‖u‖Bp,rs:=(2q​s​‖Δq​u‖Lp)ℓr<+∞.\|u\|_{B_{p,r}^{s}}:=\Big(2^{qs}\|\Delta_{q}u\|_{L^{p}}\Big)_{\ell^{r}}<+\infty.

The homogeneous Besov space B˙p,rs\dot{B}_{p,r}^{s} is defined as the set of u∈𝒮′​(ℝd)u\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) up to polynomials such that

‖u‖B˙p,rs:=(2q​s​‖Δ˙q​u‖Lp)ℓr​(ℤ)<+∞.\|u\|_{\dot{B}_{p,r}^{s}}:=\Big(2^{qs}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}u\|_{L^{p}}\Big)_{\ell^{r}(\mathbb{Z})}<+\infty.

For s,s′∈ℝs,s^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R} and p,r∈[1,∞]p,r\in[1,\infty] we define the generalized Besov space Bp,rs,s′B_{p,r}^{s,s^{\prime}} as the set of tempered distributions uu such that

‖u‖Bp,rs,s′:=(2q​s​(|q|+1)s′​‖Δq​u‖Lp)ℓr<∞\|u\|_{B_{p,r}^{s,s^{\prime}}}:=\Big(2^{qs}(|q|+1)^{s^{\prime}}\|\Delta_{q}u\|_{L^{p}}\Big)_{\ell^{r}}<\infty

Let T>0T>0 and ρ≥1,\rho\geq 1, we denote by LTρ​Bp,rs,s′L^{\rho}_{T}B_{p,r}^{s,s^{\prime}} the space of distributions uu such that

‖u‖LTρ​Bp,rs,s′:=‖(2q​s​(|q|+1)s′​‖Δq​u‖Lp)ℓr‖LTρ<+∞.\|u\|_{L^{\rho}_{T}B_{p,r}^{s,s^{\prime}}}:=\Big\|\Big(2^{qs}(|q|+1)^{s^{\prime}}\|\Delta_{q}u\|_{L^{p}}\Big)_{\ell^{r}}\Big\|_{L^{\rho}_{T}}<+\infty.

We say that uu belongs to the space L~Tρ​Bp,rs,s′\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{T}{B_{p,r}^{s,s^{\prime}}} if

‖u‖L~Tρ​Bp,rs:=(2q​s​(|q|+1)s′​‖Δq​u‖LTρ​Lp)ℓr<+∞.\|u\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{T}{B_{p,r}^{s}}}:=\Big(2^{qs}(|q|+1)^{s^{\prime}}\|\Delta_{q}u\|_{L^{\rho}_{T}L^{p}}\Big)_{\ell^{r}}<+\infty.

By a direct application of the Minkowski inequality, we have the following links between these spaces. Let ε>0,\varepsilon>0, then

LTρ​Bp,rs↪L~Tρ​Bp,rs↪LTρ​Bp,rs−ε,ifr≥ρ,L^{\rho}_{T}B_{p,r}^{s}\hookrightarrow\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{T}{B_{p,r}^{s}}\hookrightarrow{L^{\rho}_{T}}{B_{p,r}^{s-\varepsilon}},\,\textnormal{if}\quad r\geq\rho,
LTρ​Bp,rs+ε↪L~Tρ​Bp,rs↪LTρ​Bp,rs,ifρ≥r.{L^{\rho}_{T}}{B_{p,r}^{s+\varepsilon}}\hookrightarrow\widetilde{L}^{\rho}_{T}{B_{p,r}^{s}}\hookrightarrow L^{\rho}_{T}B_{p,r}^{s},\,\textnormal{if}\quad\rho\geq r.

We will make continuous use of Bernstein inequalities (see [6] for instance).

There exists a constant CC such that for q,k∈ℕ,q,k\in\mathbb{N}, 1≤a≤b1\leq a\leq b and for f∈La​(ℝd)f\in L^{a}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

sup|α|=k‖∂αSq​f‖Lb\displaystyle\sup_{|\alpha|=k}\|\partial^{\alpha}S_{q}f\|_{L^{b}} ≤\displaystyle\leq Ck​ 2q⁡(k+d⁡(1a−1b))​‖Sq​f‖La,\displaystyle C^{k}\,2^{q(k+d(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b}))}\|S_{q}f\|_{L^{a}},
C−k​2q​k​‖Δq​f‖La\displaystyle\ C^{-k}2^{qk}\|{\Delta}_{q}f\|_{L^{a}} ≤\displaystyle\leq sup|α|=k‖∂αΔq​f‖La≤Ck​2q​k​‖Δq​f‖La.\displaystyle\sup_{|\alpha|=k}\|\partial^{\alpha}{\Delta}_{q}f\|_{L^{a}}\leq C^{k}2^{qk}\|{\Delta}_{q}f\|_{L^{a}}.

3. Maximum principle

Our task is to establish some useful estimates for the following equation generalizing (1)

(6) {∂tθ+v⋅∇θ+|D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|)​θ=fdiv​v=0θ|t=0=θ0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}\theta+v\cdot\nabla\theta+\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}\theta=f\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ \theta_{|t=0}=\theta_{0},\end{array}\right.

Two special problems will be studied: the first one deals with LpL^{p} estimates that give in particular Theorem 1.1. However the second one consists in establishing some logarithmic estimates in Besov spaces with index regularity zero. The first main result of this section generalizes Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 3.1.

Let p∈[1,∞],β∈]0,1],α≥0p\in[1,\infty],\beta\in]0,1],\alpha\geq 0 and λ≥e3+2​αβ\lambda\geq e^{\frac{3+2\alpha}{\beta}}. Then any smooth solution of (6) satisfies

‖θ⁡(t)‖Lp≤‖θ0‖Lp+∫0t‖f⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ.\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|f(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau.

The proof will be done in two steps. The first one is to valid the result for the free fractional heat equation. More precisely we will establish that the semigroup et​ℒe^{t\mathcal{L}}, with ℒ:=|D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|)\mathcal{L}:=\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}, is a contraction in Lebesgue spaces LpL^{p}, for every p∈[1,∞[p\in[1,\infty[ of course under suitable conditions on the parameters α,β,λ\alpha,\beta,\lambda. This problem is reduced to show that ‖Kt‖L1≤1\|K_{t}\|_{L^{1}}\leq 1. This is equivalent to Kt∈L1K_{t}\in L^{1} and Kt≥0.K_{t}\geq 0. As we will see, to get the integrability of the kernel we do not need any restriction on the value of our parameters. Nevertheless, the positivity of KtK_{t} requires some restrictions which are detailed in Theorem 3.1. The second step is to establish the LpL^{p} estimate for the system (6) and for this purpose we use some results about Lévy operators or more generally sub-Markovians operators.

3.1. Definite positive functions

As we will see there is a strong connection between the positivity of the kernel KtK_{t} introduced above and the notion of definite positive functions. We will first gather some well-known properties about definite positive functions and recall some useful criteria for characteristic functions. Second and as an application we will show that the kernel KtK_{t} is positive under suitable conditions on the involved parameters.

Definition 3.2.

Let f:ℝd→ℂf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} be a complex-valued function. We say that ff is definite positive if only if for every integer n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*} and every set of points {xj,j=1,…,n}\{x_{j},j=1,...,n\} of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} the matrix (f⁡(xj−xk))1≤j,k≤n(f(x_{j}-x_{k}))_{1\leq j,k\leq n} is positive Hermitian, that is, for every complex numbers ξ1,…,ξn\xi_{1},...,\xi_{n} we have

∑j,k=1nf⁡(xj−xk)​ξj​ξ¯k≥0.\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}f(x_{j}-x_{k})\xi_{j}\bar{\xi}_{k}\geq 0.

We will give some results about definite positive functions.

  1. (1)

    From the definition, every definite positive function ff satisfies

    f⁡(0)≥0,f⁡(−x)=f⁡(x)¯,|f⁡(x)|≤f⁡(0).f(0)\geq 0,\quad f(-x)=\overline{f(x)},\quad|f(x)|\leq f(0).
  2. (2)

    The continuity of a definite positive function ff at zero gives the continuity everywhere. More precisely we have

    |f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)|≤2​f​(0)​(f⁡(0)−f⁡(x−y)).|f(x)-f(y)|\leq 2f(0)\big(f(0)-f(x-y)\big).
  3. (3)

    The sum of two definite positive functions is also definite positive and according to Shur’s lemma the product of two definite positive functions is also definite positive and therefore the class of definite positive functions is a convex cone closed under multiplication.

  4. (4)

    Let μ\mu be a finite positive measure then its Fourier-Stielitjes transform is given by

    μ^(ξ)=∫ℝde−ix⋅ξdμ(x).\widehat{\mu}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-ix\cdot\xi}d\mu(x).

    It is easy to see that μ^\widehat{\mu} is a definite positive function. Indeed

    ∑j,k=1nμ^​(xj−xk)​ξj​ξ¯k\displaystyle\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}\widehat{\mu}(x_{j}-x_{k})\xi_{j}\bar{\xi}_{k} =\displaystyle= ∫ℝd(∑j,k=1ne−ix⋅xjξjei​x⋅xkξ¯k)dμ(x)\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Big(\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}e^{-ix\cdot x_{j}}\xi_{j}e^{ix\cdot x_{k}}\bar{\xi}_{k}\Big)d\mu(x)
    =\displaystyle= ∫ℝd|∑j=1ne−ix⋅xjξj|2dμ(x)\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{-ix\cdot x_{j}}\xi_{j}\Big|^{2}d\mu(x)
    ≥\displaystyle\geq 0.\displaystyle 0.

The converse of the last point (4)(4) is stated by the following result due to Bochner, see for instance Theorem 19 in [3].

Theorem 3.3 (Bochner’s theorem).

Let f:ℝd→ℂf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} be a continuous definite positive function, then ff is the Fourier transform of a finite positive Borel measure.

Hereafter we will focus on a the class of radial definite positive functions. First we say that f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is radial if f⁡(x)=F⁡(|x|)f(x)=F(|x|) with F:[0,+∞[→ℂF:[0,+\infty[\to\mathbb{C}. There are some criteria for radial functions to be definite positive. For example in dimension one the celebrated criterion of Pólya [26] states that if F:[0,+∞[→ℝF:[0,+\infty[\to\mathbb{R} is continuous and convex with F⁡(0)=1F(0)=1 and limr→+∞F⁡(r)=0\lim_{r\to+\infty}F(r)=0 then f⁡(x)=F⁡(|x|)f(x)=F(|x|) is definite positive. This criterion was extended in higher dimensions by numerous authors [1, 12, 30]. We will restrict ourselves to the following one due to Askey [1].

Theorem 3.4 (Askey).

Let d∈ℕ,F:[0,+∞→ℝd\in\mathbb{N},\,\,F:[0,+\infty\to\mathbb{R} be a continuous function such that

  1. (1)

    F⁡(0)=1,F(0)=1,

  2. (2)

    the function r↦(−1)d​F(d)​(r)r\mapsto(-1)^{d}F^{(d)}(r) exists and is convex on ]0,+∞[,]0,+\infty[,

  3. (3)

    l​i​mr→+∞​F​(r)=limr→+∞F(d)​(r)=0.lim_{r\to+\infty}F(r)=\lim_{r\to+\infty}F^{(d)}(r)=0.

Then for every k∈{1,2,..,2d+1}k\in\{1,2,..,2d+1\} the function x↦F⁡(|x|)x\mapsto F(|x|) is the Fourier transform of a probability measure on ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}.

Remark 3.5.

As an application of Askey’s theorem we have that x↦e−t​|x|βx\mapsto e^{-t|x|^{\beta}} is definite positive for all t>0,t>0, β∈]0,1]\beta\in]0,1] and d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}. Although the case β∈]1,2]\beta\in]1,2] can not be reached by this criterion the result is still true.

3.2. Structure of the semigroup (e−t​|D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|))t≥0(e^{-t\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}})_{t\geq 0}

We will first recall the notions of C0−C_{0}-semigroup and sub-Markovian generators. First we introduce the notion of strongly continuous semigroup.

Definition 3.10.

Let XX be a Banach space and (Tt)t≥0(T_{t})_{t\geq 0} be a family of bounded operators from XX into XX. This family is called a strongly continuous semigroup on XX or a C0C_{0}-semigroup if

  1. (1)

    T0=Id,T_{0}=\hbox{Id},

  2. (2)

    for every t,s≥0,Tt+s=Tt​Ts,t,s\geq 0,\,T_{t+s}=T_{t}T_{s},

  3. (3)

    for every x∈X,limt→0+‖Tt​x−x‖=0.x\in X,\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}\|T_{t}x-x\|=0.

If in addition the semigroup satisfies the estimate

‖Tt‖ℒ⁡(X)≤1,\|T_{t}\|_{\mathcal{L}(X)}\leq 1,

then it is called a C0C_{0}-semigroup of contractions.

For a given C0C_{0}-semigroup of contractions (Tt)t≥0(T_{t})_{t\geq 0} we define its domain 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) by

𝒟⁡(A):={f∈X;limt→0+Tt​f−ft​exists in​X},\mathcal{D}(A):=\Big\{f\in X;\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}\frac{T_{t}f-f}{t}\,\,\textnormal{exists in}\,\,X\Big\},
A​f=limt→0+Tt​f−ft,f∈𝒟⁡(A).Af=\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}\frac{T_{t}f-f}{t},\quad f\in\mathcal{D}(A).

It is well-known that the operator AA is densely defined: its domain 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) is dense in X.X.

We introduce now the special case of sub-Markovian semigroups.

Definition 3.11.

Let X=Lp​(ℝd),X=L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), with p∈[1,∞[p\in[1,\infty[ and d∈ℕ∗.d\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Let (Tt)t≥0(T_{t})_{t\geq 0} be a C0C_{0}-semigroup of contractions on X.X. It is said a sub-Markovian semigroup if

  1. (1)

    If f∈X,f⁡(x)≥0,f\in X,f(x)\geq 0, a .e. then for every t≥0t\geq 0, Tt​f​(x)≥0,T_{t}f(x)\geq 0, a.e.,

  2. (2)

    If f∈X,|f|≤1f\in X,|f|\leq 1 then for every t≥0,|Tt​f|≤1t\geq 0,\,|T_{t}f|\leq 1.

Denote by L+p:={f∈Lp;f(x)≥0,a.e}L^{p}_{+}:=\Big\{f\in L^{p};f(x)\geq 0,a.e\Big\}. Then we have the following classical result.

Theorem 3.12 (Beurling-Deny theorem).

Let AA be a nonnegative self-adjoint operator of L2L^{2}. Then we have the equivalence between

    ∀t>0,f∈L+2⇒e−t​A​f∈L+2.\forall t>0,\,f\in L^{2}_{+}\Rightarrow e^{-tA}f\in L^{2}_{+}.

  2. (2)

    f∈𝒟⁡(A12)⇒|f|∈𝒟⁡(A12)and‖A12​|f|‖L2≤‖A12​f‖L2f\in\mathcal{D}(A^{\frac{1}{2}})\Rightarrow|f|\in\mathcal{D}(A^{\frac{1}{2}})\quad\hbox{and}\quad\|A^{\frac{1}{2}}|f|\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|A^{\frac{1}{2}}f\|_{L^{2}}

Now we will establish the following result.

Proposition 3.13.

Let d∈{1,2,3},p∈[1,∞[,α≥0,β∈]0,1]d\in\{1,2,3\},\,p\in[1,\infty[,\alpha\geq 0,\beta\in]0,1] and λ≥e3+2​αβ\lambda\geq e^{\frac{3+2\alpha}{\beta}}. Define ℒ:=|D|βlogα⁡(λ+|D|)\mathcal{L}:=\frac{|\textnormal{D}|^{\beta}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}, then

  1. (1)

    The family (e−t​ℒ)t≥0(e^{-t\mathcal{L}})_{t\geq 0} defines a C0C_{0}-semigroup of contractions in Lp​(ℝd).L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

    The operator (e−t​ℒ)t≥0(e^{-t\mathcal{L}})_{t\geq 0} satisfies the Beurling-Deny theorem described in Theorem 3.12.

Proof.

3.3. Logarithmic estimate

Let us now move to the last part of this section which deals with some logarithmic estimates generalizing the results of [31, 13]. First we recall the following result of propagation of Besov regularities.

Proposition 3.15.

Let κ≥0\kappa\geq 0 and AA be a C0C_{0} semigroup of contractions on Lm​(ℝd)L^{m}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) for every m∈[1,∞[.m\in[1,\infty[. The main goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.3. Some preliminaries lemmas will be needed. The first one is a Stroock-Varopoulos inequality for sub-Markovian operators. For the proof see [22, 23].

Let p>1p>1 and AA be a sub-Markovian generator, then we have

4​p−1p2​‖A12​(|f|p2​sign ​f)‖L22≤∫ℝd(A​f)​|f|p−1​sign​f​𝑑x≤Cp​‖A12​(|f|p2​sign ​f)‖L22.4\frac{p-1}{p^{2}}\|A^{\frac{1}{2}}(|f|^{\frac{p}{2}}\textnormal{sign }f)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(Af)\,|f|^{p-1}\textnormal{sign}\,fdx\leq C_{p}\|A^{\frac{1}{2}}(|f|^{\frac{p}{2}}\textnormal{sign }f)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

5. Commutator estimates

We will establish in this section some commutator estimates. The following result was proved in [15].

Lemma 5.1.

Given (p,m)∈[1,∞]2(p,m)\in[1,\infty]^{2} such that p≥m′p\geq m^{\prime} with m′m^{\prime} the conjugate exponent of mm. Let f,gf,g and hh be three functions such that ∇f∈Lp,g∈Lm\nabla f\in L^{p},g\in L^{m} and x​h∈Lm′xh\in L^{m^{\prime}}. Then,

‖h⋆(f​g)−f⁡(h⋆g)‖Lp≤‖x​h‖Lm′​‖∇f‖Lp​‖g‖Lm.\|h\star(fg)-f(h\star g)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|xh\|_{L^{m^{\prime}}}\|\nabla f\|_{L^{p}}\|g\|_{L^{m}}.

Now we will prove the following lemma.

Lemma 5.2.

Let (an)n∈ℤ(a_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} be a sequence of strictly nonnegative real numbers such that

M:=max⁡(supn∈ℤan−1​∑j≤naj,supn∈ℤan​∑j≥naj−1)<∞.M:=\max\Big(\sup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}a_{n}^{-1}\sum_{j\leq n}a_{j},\sup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}a_{n}\sum_{j\geq n}a_{j}^{-1}\Big)<\infty.

Then for every p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty] the linear operator T:ℓp→ℓpT:\ell^{p}\to\ell^{p} defined by

T⁡((bn)n∈ℤ)=(∑j≤naj​an−1​bj)n∈ℤT((b_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{Z}})=\Big(\sum_{j\leq n}a_{j}a_{n}^{-1}b_{j}\Big)_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}

is continuous and ‖T‖ℒ⁡(ℓp)≤M.\|T\|_{\mathcal{L}(\ell^{p})}\leq M.

By interpolation it suffices to prove the cases p=1p=1 and p=+∞p=+\infty. Let’s start with p=1p=1 and denote 𝐛=(bn)n∈ℤ.{\bf{b}}=(b_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}. Then from Fubini lemma and the hypothesis

‖T​𝐛‖ℓ1\displaystyle\|T{\bf b}\|_{\ell^{1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ∑n∈ℤ∑j≤naj​an−1​|bj|\displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{j\leq n}a_{j}a_{n}^{-1}|b_{j}|
≤\displaystyle\leq ∑j∈ℤ|bj|​aj​∑n≥jan−1\displaystyle\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}|b_{j}|a_{j}\sum_{n\geq j}a_{n}^{-1}
≤\displaystyle\leq M​‖𝐛‖ℓ1.\displaystyle M\|{\bf b}\|_{\ell^{1}}.

For the case p=+∞p=+\infty we write

‖T​𝐛‖ℓ∞\displaystyle\|T{\bf b}\|_{\ell^{\infty}} ≤\displaystyle\leq supn∈ℤ∑j≤naj​an−1​|bj|\displaystyle\sup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\sum_{j\leq n}a_{j}a_{n}^{-1}|b_{j}|
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖𝐛‖ℓ∞​supn∈ℤan−1​∑j≤naj\displaystyle\|{\bf b}\|_{\ell^{\infty}}\sup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}a_{n}^{-1}\sum_{j\leq n}a_{j}
≤\displaystyle\leq M​‖𝐛‖ℓ∞.\displaystyle M\|{\bf b}\|_{\ell^{\infty}}.

This completes the proof. ∎

In this section we will describe some smoothing effects for the model (6) and focus only on the case β=1.\beta=1. Remark that we can obtain similar results for the case β∈]0,1].\beta\in]0,1].

for every smooth solution θ\theta of (TD){\rm(TD)} with zero source term ff.

7. Proof of Theorem 1.5

Throughout this section we use the notation Φk\Phi_{k} to denote any function of the form

OPENΦk​(t)=C0​exp⁡(…​expCLOSE⏟k​t​i​m​e​s​(C0​t)​…),\Phi_{k}(t)=C_{0}\underbrace{\exp(...\exp}_{k\,times}(C_{0}t)...),

where C0C_{0} depends on the involved norms of the initial data and its value may vary from line to line up to some absolute constants. We will make an intensive use (without mentionning it) of the following trivial facts

∫0tΦk​(τ)​𝑑τ≤Φk​(t)andexp⁡(∫0tΦk​(τ)​𝑑τ)≤Φk+1​(t).\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{k}(\tau)d\tau\leq\Phi_{k}(t)\qquad{\rm and}\qquad\exp({\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{k}(\tau)d\tau})\leq\Phi_{k+1}(t).

The proof of Theorem 1.5 will be done in several steps. The first one deals with some a priori estimates for the equations (5). In the second one we prove the uniqueness part. Finally, we will discuss the construction of the solutions at the end of this section.

7.1. A priori estimates

In Theorem 1.5 we deal with critical regularities and one needs to bound the Lipschitz norm of the velocity in order to get the global persistence of the initial regularities. For this purpose we will proceed in several steps: one of the main steps is to give an L∞L^{\infty}-bound of the vorticity but due to some technical difficulties related to Riesz transforms this will not be done in a straight way. We prove before an LpL^{p} estimate for the vorticity with 2<p<∞2<p<\infty.

We will prove the following result.

Proposition 7.4.

Let α∈[0,12],λ≥e3+2​α,p∈]2,∞[\alpha\in[0,\frac{1}{2}],\lambda\geq e^{3+2\alpha},p\in]2,\infty[ and (v,θ)(v,\theta) be a smooth solution of the system (5) such that ω0,θ0,ℛα​θ0∈Lp∩L∞\omega^{0},\theta_{0},\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta_{0}\in L^{p}\cap L^{\infty}. Then we have

(30) ‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛα​θ​(t)‖L∞≤Φ3​(t)\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{3}(t)

∥Γ(t)∥L∞≤∥Γ0∥L∞+∫0t∥[ℛα,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥L∞dτ.\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\Gamma^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R}_{\alpha},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau.

then using Theorem 3.1 we get

∥ℛαθ(t)∥L∞≤∥ℛαθ(t)∥L∞+∫0t∥[ℛα,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥L∞dτ.\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R}_{\alpha},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau.

Thus we obtain

‖Γ⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛα​θ​(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ∥Γ0∥L∞+∥ℛαθ0∥L∞+2∫0t∥[ℛα,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥L∞dτ\displaystyle\|\Gamma^{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+2\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R}_{\alpha},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau
≤\displaystyle\leq C0+∫0t∥[ℛα,v⋅∇]θ(τ)∥B∞,10dτ.\displaystyle C_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\|[\mathcal{R}_{\alpha},v\cdot\nabla]\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}d\tau.

It follows from Theorem 3.1, Proposition 5.3-(2) and Proposition 7.1

‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛα​θ​(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim C0+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖L∞∩Lp​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,1ϵ+‖θ⁡(τ)‖Lp)​𝑑τ\displaystyle C_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}\cap L^{p}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}+\|\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau
≲\displaystyle\lesssim C0+‖ω‖Lt∞​Lp​(‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,1ϵ+t​‖θ0‖Lp)\displaystyle C_{0}+\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}}\big(\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}+t\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big)
+\displaystyle+ ∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖L∞​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,1ϵ+‖θ0‖Lp)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}+\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau.

Let 0<ϵ<1−2p0<\epsilon<1-\frac{2}{p} then using (29) we get

‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛα​θ​(t)‖L∞≲Φ2​(t)+∫0t‖ω⁡(τ)‖L∞​(‖θ⁡(τ)‖B∞,1ϵ+‖θ0‖Lp)​𝑑τ.\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\Phi_{2}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\|\omega(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\big(\|\theta(\tau)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{\epsilon}}+\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}\big)d\tau.

Therefore we obtain by Gronwall lemma and (29)

‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞+‖ℛα​θ​(t)‖L∞≤Φ3​(t).\displaystyle\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{3}(t).

Proof of (31). Let N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} to be chosen later. Using the fact that ‖Δ˙q​v‖L∞≈2−q​‖Δ˙q​ω‖L∞\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}v\|_{L^{\infty}}\approx 2^{-q}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}, then we get

‖v⁡(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖χ⁡(2N​|D|)​v​(t)‖L∞+∑q≥−N2−q​‖Δ˙q​ω​(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|)v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\sum_{q\geq-N}2^{-q}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖χ⁡(2N​|D|)​v​(t)‖L∞+2N​‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞.\displaystyle\|\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|)v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+2^{N}\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}.

Applying the frequency localizing operator to the velocity equation we get

χ⁡(2N​|D|)​v=χ⁡(2N​|D|)​v0+∫0t𝒫​χ​(2N​|D|)​θ​(τ)​𝑑τ+∫0t𝒫​χ​(2N​|D|)​div​(v⊗v)​(τ)​𝑑τ,\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|)v=\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|)v_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{P}\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|)\theta(\tau)d\tau+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{P}\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|){\rm div}(v\otimes v)(\tau)d\tau,

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} stands for Leray projector. From Lemma 2.1, Calderón-Zygmund estimate and the uniform boundness of χ⁡(2N​|D|)\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|) we get

∫0t‖χ⁡(2N​|D|)​𝒫​θ​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\|\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|)\mathcal{P}\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau ≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−N​2p​∫0t‖θ⁡(τ)‖Lp​𝑑τ\displaystyle 2^{-N\frac{2}{p}}\int_{0}^{t}\|\theta(\tau)\|_{L^{p}}d\tau
≲\displaystyle\lesssim t​‖θ0‖Lp.\displaystyle t\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}.

Using Proposition 3.9-(2) we find

∫0t‖𝒫​χ​(2N​|D|)​div​(v⊗v)​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ≲2N​∫0t‖v⁡(τ)‖L∞2​𝑑τ.\int_{0}^{t}\|\mathcal{P}\chi(2^{N}|\textnormal{D}|){\rm div}(v\otimes v)(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau\lesssim 2^{N}\int_{0}^{t}\|v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}d\tau.

The outcome is

‖v⁡(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖v0‖L∞+t​‖θ0‖Lp+2−N​∫0t‖v⁡(τ)‖L∞2​𝑑τ+2N​‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞\displaystyle\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}+t\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}+2^{-N}\int_{0}^{t}\|v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}d\tau+2^{N}\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim 2−N​∫0t‖v⁡(τ)‖L∞2​𝑑τ+2N​Φ3​(t)\displaystyle 2^{-N}\int_{0}^{t}\|v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}d\tau+2^{N}\Phi_{3}(t)

Choosing judiciously NN we find

‖v⁡(t)‖L∞≤Φ3​(t)​(1+(∫0t‖v⁡(τ)‖L∞2​𝑑τ)12).\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{3}(t)\Big(1+\Big(\int_{0}^{t}\|v(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}d\tau\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big).

From Gronwall lemma we get

‖v⁡(t)‖L∞≤Φ4​(t).\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{4}(t).

7.1.3. Lipschitz bound of the velocity

Now we will establish the following result.

Proposition 7.5.

Let α∈[0,12],λ≥e3+2​α,p∈]2,∞[\alpha\in[0,\frac{1}{2}],\lambda\geq e^{3+2\alpha},p\in]2,\infty[ and (v,θ)(v,\theta) be a smooth solution of the system (5) with ω0,θ0,ℛα​θ0∈B∞,10∩Lp\omega^{0},\theta_{0},\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta_{0}\in B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{p}. Then

‖ℛα​θ​(t)‖B∞,10+‖ω⁡(t)‖B∞,10+‖v⁡(t)‖B∞,11≤Φ4​(t).\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|\omega(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|v(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1}}\leq\Phi_{4}(t).

Applying Corollary 3.17 to the equations (17) and (17), we obtain

(32) ∥Γ(t)∥B∞,10+∥ℛαθ(t)∥B∞,10≲(C0+∥[ℛα,v⋅∇]θ∥Lt1​B∞,10)(1+∥∇v∥Lt1​L∞).\|\Gamma(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\theta(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\lesssim\Big(C_{0}+\big\|[\mathcal{R}_{\alpha},v\cdot\nabla]\theta\big\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\Big)\Big(1+\|\nabla v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}\Big).

≲\displaystyle\lesssim Φ2​(t)+‖ω⁡(t)‖B∞,10.\displaystyle\Phi_{2}(t)+\|\omega(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}.

Thus we obtain from Gronwall inequality

Coming back to (33) we get

‖∇v​(t)‖L∞≤Φ4​(t).\displaystyle\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Phi_{4}(t).

‖v⁡(t)‖B∞,11≤Φ4​(t)\|v(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1}}\leq\Phi_{4}(t)

7.2. Uniqueness

We will show that the Boussinesq system (5) has a unique solution in the following function space

ℰT=(LT∞​B∞,10∩LT1​B∞,11)×(LT∞​Lp∩L~T1​Bp,∞1,−α),2<p<∞.\mathcal{E}_{T}=(L^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{0}\cap L^{1}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{1})\times(L^{\infty}_{T}L^{p}\cap\widetilde{L}^{1}_{T}B_{p,\infty}^{1,-\alpha}),\quad 2<p<\infty.

v=v2−v1,θ=θ2−θ1.v=v^{2}-v^{1},\quad\theta=\theta^{2}-\theta^{1}.

Then we get

{∂tv+v2⋅∇v=−∇π−v⋅∇v1+θ​e2∂tθ+v2⋅∇θ+|D|logα⁡(λ+|D|)θ=−v⋅∇θ1v|t=0=v0,θ|t=0=θ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v^{2}\cdot\nabla v=-\nabla\pi-v\cdot\nabla v^{1}+\theta e_{2}\\ \partial_{t}\theta+v^{2}\cdot\nabla\theta+\frac{|\textnormal{D}|}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}\theta=-v\cdot\nabla\theta^{1}\\ v_{|t=0}=v_{0},\quad\theta_{|t=0}=\theta_{0}.\end{array}\right.

According to Proposition 3.15 we have

‖v⁡(t)‖B∞,10≤C​eC​V1​(t)​(‖v0‖B∞,10+‖∇π‖Lt1​B∞,10+‖v⋅∇v1‖Lt1​B∞,10+‖θ‖Lt1​B∞,10),\|v(t)\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\leq Ce^{CV_{1}(t)}\Big(\|v_{0}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|\nabla\pi\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|v\cdot\nabla v^{1}\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|\theta\|_{L^{1}_{t}B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\Big),

with V1​(t)=‖∇v1‖Lt1​L∞.V_{1}(t)=\|\nabla v^{1}\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}. Straightforward computations using the incompressibility of the flows gives

∇π\displaystyle\nabla\pi =\displaystyle= −∇Δ−1div (v⋅∇(v1+v2))+∇Δ−1∂2θ\displaystyle-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\textnormal{div }(v\cdot\nabla(v^{1}+v^{2}))+\nabla\Delta^{-1}\partial_{2}\theta
=\displaystyle= I+II.\displaystyle\hbox{I}+\hbox{II}.

To estimate the first term of the RHS we use the definition

∥I∥B∞,10≲∥(∇Δ−1div )div Δ−1(v⊗(v1+v2))∥L∞+∥v⋅∇(v1+v2)∥B∞,11\|\hbox{I}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\lesssim\|(\nabla\Delta^{-1}\textnormal{div })\textnormal{div }\Delta_{-1}(v\otimes(v^{1}+v^{2}))\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|v\cdot\nabla(v^{1}+v^{2})\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1}}

From Proposition 3.1-(2) of [15] and Besov embeddings we have

∥(∇Δ−1div )div Δ−1(v⊗(v1+v2))∥L∞\displaystyle\|(\nabla\Delta^{-1}\textnormal{div })\textnormal{div }\Delta_{-1}(v\otimes(v^{1}+v^{2}))\|_{L^{\infty}} ≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖v⊗(v1+v2)‖L∞\displaystyle\|v\otimes(v^{1}+v^{2})\|_{L^{\infty}}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖v‖B∞,10​‖v1+v2‖B∞,10.\displaystyle\|v\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\|v^{1}+v^{2}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}.

Using the incompressibility of vv and using Bony’s decomposition one can easily obtain

‖v⋅∇(v1+v2)‖B∞,10≲‖v‖B∞,10​‖v1+v2‖B∞,11.\|v\cdot\nabla(v^{1}+v^{2})\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\lesssim\|v\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\|v^{1}+v^{2}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1}}.

Putting together these estimates yields

(35) ‖I‖B∞,10≲‖v‖B∞,10​‖v1+v2‖B∞,11.\|\hbox{I}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\lesssim\|v\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}\|v^{1}+v^{2}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{1}}.

7.3. Existence

We consider the following system

(Bn) {∂tvn+vn⋅∇vn+∇πn=θn​e2∂tθn+vn⋅∇θn+|Dlogα⁡(λ+|D|)​θn=0div​vn=0vn|t=0=Snv0,θn|t=0=Snθ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v_{n}+v_{n}\cdot\nabla v_{n}+\nabla\pi_{n}=\theta_{n}e_{2}\\ \partial_{t}\theta_{n}+v_{n}\cdot\nabla\theta_{n}+\frac{|\textnormal{D}}{\log^{\alpha}(\lambda+|\textnormal{D}|)}\theta_{n}=0\\ \textnormal{div}v_{n}=0\\ {v_{n}}_{|t=0}=S_{n}v^{0},\quad{\theta_{n}}_{|t=0}=S_{n}\theta^{0}.\end{array}\right.

By using the same method as [13] we can prove that this system has a unique local smooth solution (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}). The global existence of these solutions is governed by the following criterion: we can push the construction beyond the time TT if the quantity ‖∇vn‖LT1​L∞\|\nabla v_{n}\|_{L^{1}_{T}L^{\infty}} is finite. Now from the a priori estimates the Lipschitz norm can not blow up in finite time and then the solution (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) is globally defined. Once again from the a priori estimates we have for 2<p<∞2<p<\infty

‖vn‖LT∞​B∞,11+‖ωn‖LT∞​Lp+‖θn‖LT∞​𝒳p≤Φ4​(T).\|v_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{1}}+\|\omega_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}L^{p}}+\|\theta_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}\mathcal{X}_{p}}\leq\Phi_{4}(T).

The space 𝒳p\mathcal{X}_{p} was introduced before the statement of Theorem 1.5 It follows that up to an extraction the sequence (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) is weakly convergent to (v,θ)(v,\theta) belonging to LT∞​B∞,11×LT∞​𝒳p,L^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{1}\times L^{\infty}_{T}\mathcal{X}_{p}, with ω∈LT∞​Lp\omega\in L^{\infty}_{T}L^{p}. For (n,m)∈ℕ2(n,m)\in\mathbb{N}^{2} we set vn,m=vn−vmv_{n,m}=v_{n}-v_{m} and θn,m=θn−θm\theta_{n,m}=\theta_{n}-\theta_{m} then according to the estimate (40) and (41) we get for T=δT=\delta

‖vn,m‖LT∞​B∞,10+‖θn,m‖LT1​Bp,12p≲‖Sn​v0−Sm​v0‖B∞,10+‖Sn​θ0−Sm​θ0‖Lp.\|v_{n,m}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|\theta_{n,m}\|_{L^{1}_{T}B_{p,1}^{\frac{2}{p}}}\lesssim\|S_{n}v_{0}-S_{m}v_{0}\|_{B_{\infty,1}^{0}}+\|S_{n}\theta_{0}-S_{m}\theta_{0}\|_{L^{p}}.

This shows that (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) is a Cauchy sequence in the Banach space LT∞​B∞,10×LT1​Bp,12pL^{\infty}_{T}B_{\infty,1}^{0}\times L^{1}_{T}B_{p,1}^{\frac{2}{p}} and then it converges strongly to (v,θ).(v,\theta). This allows to pass to the limit in the system (Bn)({\rm B}_{n}) and then we get that (v,θ)(v,\theta) is a solution of the Boussinesq system (5).
